**Calibration methods.** The most common calibration approach is matching the static angle of repose between DEM and experiment (girnth2024dimensionlessquantitiesin pages 5-7, ye2026digitaltwindrivenmanufacturing pages 6-7, ye2026digitaltwindrivenmanufacturing pages 7-10). Girnth et al. additionally used bulk density as a second target and measured sliding friction and restitution independently (girnth2024dimensionlessquantitiesin pages 7-9). Ye et al. validated against in-situ dynamic repose angle with <2% relative error (ye2026digitaltwindrivenmanufacturing pages 7-10). Other calibration targets reported in the literature include Hall flow time, rotating drum/Revolution powder analyser dynamic repose angle and cohesive index, shear cell unconfined yield strength, and Anton Paar powder cell torque (haapa2023simulationofmetal pages 36-38, ajabshir2024effectoftemperaturea pages 121-126, lupo2021calibrationofdem pages 2-3). Lupo et al. (2021) demonstrated that a bulk calibration approach using angle of repose alone with Hertz–Mindlin JKR could not simultaneously satisfy both angle of repose and unconfined yield strength, recommending direct measurement of interparticle surface energy when possible (lupo2021calibrationofdem pages 2-3, lupo2021calibrationofdem pages 5-7). Using at least two independent observables—ideally including one shear-dominated test resembling blade spreading—is recommended (haapa2023simulationofmetal pages 36-38).

---

### 2. Spreading Study Results

**Packing fraction vs. gap/D90.** Salehi et al. (2023) reported that continuous powder layers require a blade gap of approximately 3–4 × D90 for cohesive powders and about 2 × D90 for free-flowing powders (salehi2023optimisingspreadlayerquality pages 2-3). Increasing gap thickness from 0.01 to 0.03 mm raised packing fraction from roughly 15% to 33% (salehi2023optimisingspreadlayerquality pages 2-3). Burgess (2024) reviewed SS316L spreading at gap settings of 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, and 3 × D90 (45–135 µm for D90 = 45 µm); smaller gaps produced more voids and porosity, with quality deteriorating significantly below about 1.5 × D90 (burgess2024discreteelementmethod pages 88-94). Wang (2021) tested Hastelloy X (D90 = 52.7 µm) at gaps of 70 and 90 µm (~1.3–1.7 × D90) (wang2021particlescalemodelling pages 121-125). For AlSi10Mg with D90 ~ 60 µm, a 30–50 µm layer thickness gives gap/D90 ratios of only 0.5–0.8, which places the process in the regime where jamming and coverage degradation are significant concerns.

**Blade speed effects.** Packing fraction generally decreases with increasing spreading speed. One DEM simulation found a decline from 47% to 25% as speed rose from 10 to 100 mm/s (salehi2023optimisingspreadlayerquality pages 2-3). Brocksieper et al. (2026) found that AlSi10Mg powder layers showed notably higher surface roughness at 250 mm/s compared to 50 and 150 mm/s, particularly with blade and hopper recoaters; roller recoaters were less speed-sensitive for 316L and IN718 but still showed increased roughness for AlSi10Mg at the highest speed (brocksieper2026investigationofflowability pages 7-9). The literature converges on the finding that lower spreading speeds (typically 20–50 mm/s) produce more uniform, denser powder beds with fewer voids and lower surface roughness (haydari2021thespreadingbehaviour pages 46-48, haydari2021thespreadingbehaviour pages 51-54, burgess2024discreteelementmethod pages 88-94).

**Blade type comparisons.** Roller spreaders generally produce denser, smoother layers than rigid blades due to their larger contact area and gradual compaction effect (haydari2021thespreadingbehaviour pages 46-48, haydari2021thespreadingbehaviour pages 51-54, salehi2023optimisingspreadlayerquality pages 2-3). Brocksieper et al. confirmed that the roller recoater consistently produced the lowest arithmetic mean roughness Sa across all three tested powders, while the hopper recoater produced the highest Sa with characteristic grooves (brocksieper2026investigationofflowability pages 7-9). Among blade geometries, wide-nose or flat-bottomed blades outperformed sharp-edged blades, as the rounded leading edge applies downward force and the flat trailing surface promotes particle settling (salehi2023optimisingspreadlayerquality pages 12-13). Steel blades produced better coverage than silicone or ceramic blades (haydari2021thespreadingbehaviour pages 48-51).

**Critical gap and jamming.** Below approximately 1–1.5 × D90, particle jamming, mechanical arching, streaks, and empty patches become frequent (haydari2021thespreadingbehaviour pages 46-48, burgess2024discreteelementmethod pages 88-94, burgess2024discreteelementmethod pages 85-88). A critical blade height exists below which mass flow is zero because particles jam or their diameters exceed the gap (burgess2024discreteelementmethod pages 85-88). For AlSi10Mg with D90 ~ 60 µm, spreading at 30 µm nominal layer thickness (gap/D90 ~ 0.5) is well into the jamming-prone regime.

**Effective layer thickness after melt shrinkage.** Lu et al. (2026) developed a mathematical model showing that the steady-state effective powder stacking height approaches H_s = H/δ, where H is the nominal layer thickness (platform drop) and δ is the effective packing/densification ratio (~0.6 for the studied powder), yielding H_s ≈ 1.667H (lu2026exploringtheactual pages 8-12, lu2026exploringtheactual pages 12-16, lu2026exploringtheactual pages 16-19). For a nominal 30 µm layer, the steady-state powder bed height stabilizes at approximately 50 µm after about 25 layers (lu2026exploringtheactual pages 12-16). The total volumetric shrinkage was reported as approximately 40%, comprising 31.5% from liquid-metal infiltration into powder-bed voids and 8.5% from solidification contraction (lu2026exploringtheactual pages 16-19, lu2026exploringtheactual pages 6-8). Elton et al. (2023) similarly found that melting randomly packed powder (~50–60% solid fraction) produces a consolidated layer of approximately 50–60% of the nominal powder-layer thickness (elton2023electrostaticpowderspreading pages 14-19). The relationship is layer_effective = packing_density × nominal_powder_height; the steady-state consolidated thickness equals the nominal platform drop H once the powder bed reaches equilibrium (bogdanova2024mesoscalesimulationof pages 10-13).

**Granular Bond number.** Spierings (2018) defined the cohesive granular Bond number as BN = F_interparticle/F_gravity, noting that increasing fine-particle content raises BN and reduces flowability (spierings2018powderspreadabilityand pages 115-119). However, explicit numerical Bond number values for 20–63 µm AlSi10Mg were not found in the retrieved literature. For the particle sizes of interest (D50 ~ 35–40 µm, density ~2700 kg/m³), van der Waals adhesion forces become comparable to gravitational forces, placing these powders in the transitional regime (BN ~ 0.1–1) between free-flowing and cohesive behavior.

**Hausner ratio.** Gas-atomised AlSi10Mg showed a Hausner ratio of 1.06, with apparent density 1.40 g/cm³ and tapped density 1.50 g/cm³ (kraner2020characterizationofnonferrous pages 2-3). This value indicates "good" to "excellent" flowability on the Carr classification scale. However, Hausner ratio alone may not predict spreadability, as Spierings noted poor correlation between Hausner ratio and observed powder-layer quality in several cases (spierings2018powderspreadabilityand pages 115-119).

**Angle of repose and avalanche angle.** Values for AlSi10Mg vary dramatically with test geometry: Kraner measured 45° using a standard ASTM method (kraner2020characterizationofnonferrous pages 2-3), while Girnth et al. measured 60.73° ± 4.62° using a miniaturized setup with a 500 µm orifice and 5 mm table (girnth2024dimensionlessquantitiesin pages 7-9). For AlSi7Mg powders, static angles ranged from 26° to 39° depending on PSD and morphology (munizlerma2018acomprehensiveapproach pages 8-11). Untreated fine aluminium powder gave a 60° angle of repose, reduced to 24–32° by silane surface treatment (chen2010characterizationofparticle pages 6-8). These large variations underscore the importance of matching test geometry to the DEM calibration setup.

**Humidity, oxide, and drying effects.** Aluminium powders are particularly sensitive to environmental conditions due to their native Al₂O₃ oxide layer, which increases surface roughness and interparticle friction (rezaei2026powderdegradationand pages 24-25). Fine aluminium particles (<20 µm) are most susceptible to moisture uptake, which promotes adhesion, agglomeration, poor spreading, and non-uniform layers (rezaei2026powderdegradationand pages 24-25). The fine AlSi7Mg powder (D50 = 31 µm) with higher surface area showed substantially greater moisture/vapor sorption than coarser fractions, increasing surface energy heterogeneity and work of cohesion (munizlerma2018acomprehensiveapproach pages 8-11). Surface modification—particularly silane treatment—reduced surface free energy from 123 mJ/m² to 19.9–30 mJ/m² for fine aluminium, with corresponding reductions in angle of repose from 60° to 24–32° (chen2010characterizationofparticle pages 6-8). Drying at ~200°C under vacuum for 2 hours is a standard conditioning step for AM aluminium powders; sieving out fines, inert-atmosphere handling, and dry storage are also recommended to maintain flowability (rezaei2026powderdegradationand pages 24-25, munizlerma2018acomprehensiveapproach pages 5-8).

### 4. Dose Factor Recommendations and Hopper Flow

**Dose factor and effective layer thickness.** The dose factor (ratio of powder volume dispensed to the nominal layer volume on the build area) must compensate for powder-bed porosity and spreading losses. The Lu et al. (2026) model predicts that the steady-state effective powder-bed height is H/δ ≈ 1.67H for δ = 0.6 (lu2026exploringtheactual pages 8-12, lu2026exploringtheactual pages 12-16). This implies that a minimum dose factor of approximately 1/δ ≈ 1.67 is required to avoid "short feed" (insufficient powder reaching the far end of the build plate). In practice, dose factors of 1.5–2.0 as planned are consistent with this requirement, providing a margin for spreading losses, edge effects, and powder-pile depletion across the build width. When the dose is insufficient ("short feed"), the powder pile is exhausted before the blade traverses the full build area, resulting in bare or thin regions on the far side of the build plate, reduced packing density, and voids that lead to lack-of-fusion defects.

**Hopper flow of fine Al powder.** Fine aluminium powders (20–63 µm) present significant hopper flow challenges. Jenike analysis uses cohesive strength from a flow-function test and wall friction to calculate the minimum outlet size for arching prevention and the hopper angle for mass flow (maynard2013tenstepsto pages 2-4, maynard2013tenstepsto pages 4-5). For mass flow, the hopper walls must be sufficiently steep with low wall friction; a commonly cited 60° conical hopper angle from horizontal is generally insufficient to guarantee mass flow (maynard2013tenstepsto pages 2-4). Mass flow requires that the hopper slope be steep enough that material flows along the walls whenever solids are withdrawn, preventing stagnant zones that lead to ratholing (maynard2013tenstepsto pages 2-4). For funnel-flow self-cleaning, the hopper slope should be 15–20° steeper than the wall-friction angle (maynard2013tenstepsto pages 4-5).

**Bridging and ratholing in narrow outlets.** For a slot outlet of approximately 8 mm width, fine cohesive aluminium powder is at significant risk of arching/bridging, as the critical arching dimension for cohesive powders in this size range can exceed the outlet width. The minimum outlet width depends on the material's unconfined yield strength at the consolidation stress in the hopper, requiring direct shear cell measurement. For fine metal powders, permeability-based analysis is essential because standard coarse-powder discharge equations do not account for resistance to airflow through the fine powder bed (maynard2013tenstepsto pages 4-5). Stainless-steel hoppers provide relatively low wall friction angles (typically 15–25° for polished stainless against metal powders), which is favorable for mass flow, but the wall angle must still be verified against measured wall friction for the specific aluminium powder (maynard2013tenstepsto pages 2-4).

---

### 5. Powder Migration into Gaps and Seals

Published literature on powder migration into radial clearances around build plates and pistons in LPBF machines is limited, as this is primarily proprietary machine design knowledge. The build platform typically moves within a close-fitting build sleeve, and the dosing piston moves within a dosing sleeve (EP3363566B1 pages 5-6). For fine metal powders with particles as small as 20 µm, radial clearances of 0.1–0.4 mm represent gaps that are several particle diameters wide, allowing significant powder migration under the combined effects of gravity, vibration from the recoater, and gas flow.

**Seal types.** Deridov (2024) described the use of acrylic felt as a piston powder seal for a prototype SLS machine where elevated temperatures were not a concern, and specified wool felt for a functional high-temperature machine to prevent burning (deridov2024analysisofpowder pages 31-36). The patent by McMurtry (EP3363566B1) describes build platform and dosing piston arrangements within sleeves but does not detail specific sealing elements in the retrieved sections (EP3363566B1 pages 5-6). In practice, commercial LPBF machines employ various sealing strategies including felt strip seals (compressed between the piston periphery and the sleeve), brush seals (bristle rows that conform to the gap while allowing piston motion), labyrinth grooves machined into the piston or sleeve that trap powder in successive channels, and close-tolerance machined fits that rely on the powder's own bridging behavior in narrow gaps (<0.1 mm). O-rings and elastomeric seals are less common due to thermal constraints, powder abrasion, and the need for very low friction during precise vertical positioning.

**Design considerations.** The minimum clearance is constrained by thermal expansion (the build plate and sleeve heat differentially during processing), mechanical tolerances, and the need to avoid binding. With aluminium alloy builds, the lower processing temperatures compared to steel or nickel alloys reduce differential thermal expansion, potentially allowing tighter clearances. However, the light density and fine particle size of Al powders make them particularly prone to migration compared to denser materials. Pressurized inert gas flow in the build chamber can either aid or hinder powder migration depending on flow direction relative to the gap. Periodic cleaning and maintenance protocols are essential, as accumulated powder in the piston mechanism can cause binding, positional errors, and contamination of subsequent builds.

### Summary of Recommended DEM Input Parameters for LIGGGHTS Simulations

For the user's planned LIGGGHTS simulations of AlSi10Mg spreading with Hertz–Mindlin and simplified JKR cohesion, the following starting parameters are suggested based on the literature synthesis:

- **Young's modulus:** Scale to ~75 MPa (10⁻³ × E_real), verifying that maximum overlaps remain <0.5% of particle radius (girnth2024dimensionlessquantitiesin pages 9-11, ye2026digitaltwindrivenmanufacturing pages 6-7)
- **Poisson ratio:** 0.33 (girnth2024dimensionlessquantitiesin pages 9-11)
- **Density:** 2670–2680 kg/m³ (girnth2024dimensionlessquantitiesin pages 9-11, ye2026digitaltwindrivenmanufacturing pages 7-10)
- **Coefficient of restitution:** 0.54–0.64 (girnth2024dimensionlessquantitiesin pages 7-9, ye2026digitaltwindrivenmanufacturing pages 7-10)
- **Sliding friction:** 0.2–0.67 (measured values vary with surface condition; start with ~0.3–0.4 and calibrate) (girnth2024dimensionlessquantitiesin pages 7-9, ye2026digitaltwindrivenmanufacturing pages 7-10)
- **Rolling friction:** 0.05–0.12 (calibrate against angle of repose and/or bulk density) (girnth2024dimensionlessquantitiesin pages 9-11, ye2026digitaltwindrivenmanufacturing pages 7-10)
- **JKR cohesion energy density:** 0.5–3.5 mJ/m² (start with ~0.8–1.5 mJ/m² and calibrate against angle of repose and spreading tests) (girnth2024dimensionlessquantitiesin pages 9-11, ye2026digitaltwindrivenmanufacturing pages 7-10)
- **Calibration targets:** Static angle of repose plus at least one additional test (bulk density, Hall flow, shear cell, or in-situ dynamic repose angle) (haapa2023simulationofmetal pages 36-38, girnth2024dimensionlessquantitiesin pages 5-7, ye2026digitaltwindrivenmanufacturing pages 7-10, lupo2021calibrationofdem pages 2-3)

### 2. Spreading Study Results

**Packing fraction vs. gap/D90.** Salehi et al. (2023) reported that continuous powder layers require a blade gap of approximately 3–4 × D90 for cohesive powders and about 2 × D90 for free-flowing powders (pqac-00000007). Increasing gap thickness from 0.01 to 0.03 mm raised packing fraction from roughly 15% to 33% (pqac-00000007). Burgess (2024) reviewed SS316L spreading at gap settings of 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, and 3 × D90 (45–135 µm for D90 = 45 µm); smaller gaps produced more voids and porosity, with quality deteriorating significantly below about 1.5 × D90 (pqac-00000008). Wang (2021) tested Hastelloy X (D90 = 52.7 µm) at gaps of 70 and 90 µm (~1.3–1.7 × D90) (pqac-00000010). For AlSi10Mg with D90 ~ 60 µm, a 30–50 µm layer thickness gives gap/D90 ratios of only 0.5–0.8, which places the process in the regime where jamming and coverage degradation are significant concerns.

**Blade speed effects.** Packing fraction generally decreases with increasing spreading speed. One DEM simulation found a decline from 47% to 25% as speed rose from 10 to 100 mm/s (pqac-00000007). Brocksieper et al. (2026) found that AlSi10Mg powder layers showed notably higher surface roughness at 250 mm/s compared to 50 and 150 mm/s, particularly with blade and hopper recoaters; roller recoaters were less speed-sensitive for 316L and IN718 but still showed increased roughness for AlSi10Mg at the highest speed (pqac-00000040). The literature converges on the finding that lower spreading speeds (typically 20–50 mm/s) produce more uniform, denser powder beds with fewer voids and lower surface roughness (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000006, pqac-00000008).

**Blade type comparisons.** Roller spreaders generally produce denser, smoother layers than rigid blades due to their larger contact area and gradual compaction effect (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000006, pqac-00000007). Brocksieper et al. confirmed that the roller recoater consistently produced the lowest arithmetic mean roughness Sa across all three tested powders, while the hopper recoater produced the highest Sa with characteristic grooves (pqac-00000040). Among blade geometries, wide-nose or flat-bottomed blades outperformed sharp-edged blades, as the rounded leading edge applies downward force and the flat trailing surface promotes particle settling (pqac-00000011). Steel blades produced better coverage than silicone or ceramic blades (pqac-00000012).

**Critical gap and jamming.** Below approximately 1–1.5 × D90, particle jamming, mechanical arching, streaks, and empty patches become frequent (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009). A critical blade height exists below which mass flow is zero because particles jam or their diameters exceed the gap (pqac-00000009). For AlSi10Mg with D90 ~ 60 µm, spreading at 30 µm nominal layer thickness (gap/D90 ~ 0.5) is well into the jamming-prone regime.

**Effective layer thickness after melt shrinkage.** Lu et al. (2026) developed a mathematical model showing that the steady-state effective powder stacking height approaches H_s = H/δ, where H is the nominal layer thickness (platform drop) and δ is the effective packing/densification ratio (~0.6 for the studied powder), yielding H_s ≈ 1.667H (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000015, pqac-00000017). For a nominal 30 µm layer, the steady-state powder bed height stabilizes at approximately 50 µm after about 25 layers (pqac-00000015). The total volumetric shrinkage was reported as approximately 40%, comprising 31.5% from liquid-metal infiltration into powder-bed voids and 8.5% from solidification contraction (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000018). Elton et al. (2023) similarly found that melting randomly packed powder (~50–60% solid fraction) produces a consolidated layer of approximately 50–60% of the nominal powder-layer thickness (pqac-00000013). The relationship is layer_effective = packing_density × nominal_powder_height; the steady-state consolidated thickness equals the nominal platform drop H once the powder bed reaches equilibrium (pqac-00000016).

---

### 3. Cohesion Metrics for 20–63 µm Al Powders

The following table compiles measured cohesion and flowability data for AlSi10Mg and related aluminium alloy powders.

| Property | Value | Powder/source | Reference |

| Hausner ratio | 1.06 | Gas-atomised AlSi10Mg; apparent density 1.40 g/cm³ and tapped density 1.50 g/cm³ | Kraner et al. (2020) (pqac-00000045) |
| Hausner ratio | 1.03–1.15 | Six non-ferrous powders, including Al, AlSi12, AlSi10Mg, and Cu | Kraner et al. (2020) (pqac-00000045) |
| Hausner ratio | <1.25 for most powders tested | Fine AM powders; values concerned mainly Fe- and Ni-based powders, so this is contextual rather than Al-specific | Spierings (2018) (pqac-00000030) |
| Static angle of repose | 45° | Gas-atomised AlSi10Mg | Kraner et al. (2020) (pqac-00000045) |
| Static angle of repose | 60.73° ± 4.62° | AlSi10Mg discharged through a 500 µm orifice onto a 5 mm-diameter table; strongly geometry-dependent result | Girnth et al. (2024) (pqac-00000038) |

| Spread-layer roughness, Sa | Higher on average than 316L and Alloy 718 | AlSi10Mg spread using blade, roller, and hopper recoaters at 50, 150, and 250 mm/s; roller layers were generally smoothest, while 250 mm/s notably increased AlSi10Mg roughness | Brocksieper et al. (2026) (pqac-00000040) |


*Table: Published cohesion, flowability, density, and spread-layer metrics for AlSi10Mg and related aluminium alloy powders. Test geometry and parameter definitions vary, so values should be compared only under matched methods.*

**Granular Bond number.** Spierings (2018) defined the cohesive granular Bond number as BN = F_interparticle/F_gravity, noting that increasing fine-particle content raises BN and reduces flowability (pqac-00000030). However, explicit numerical Bond number values for 20–63 µm AlSi10Mg were not found in the retrieved literature. For the particle sizes of interest (D50 ~ 35–40 µm, density ~2700 kg/m³), van der Waals adhesion forces become comparable to gravitational forces, placing these powders in the transitional regime (BN ~ 0.1–1) between free-flowing and cohesive behavior.

**Hausner ratio.** Gas-atomised AlSi10Mg showed a Hausner ratio of 1.06, with apparent density 1.40 g/cm³ and tapped density 1.50 g/cm³ (pqac-00000045). This value indicates "good" to "excellent" flowability on the Carr classification scale. However, Hausner ratio alone may not predict spreadability, as Spierings noted poor correlation between Hausner ratio and observed powder-layer quality in several cases (pqac-00000030).

**Angle of repose and avalanche angle.** Values for AlSi10Mg vary dramatically with test geometry: Kraner measured 45° using a standard ASTM method (pqac-00000045), while Girnth et al. measured 60.73° ± 4.62° using a miniaturized setup with a 500 µm orifice and 5 mm table (pqac-00000038). For AlSi7Mg powders, static angles ranged from 26° to 39° depending on PSD and morphology (pqac-00000031). Untreated fine aluminium powder gave a 60° angle of repose, reduced to 24–32° by silane surface treatment (pqac-00000032). These large variations underscore the importance of matching test geometry to the DEM calibration setup.

**Humidity, oxide, and drying effects.** Aluminium powders are particularly sensitive to environmental conditions due to their native Al₂O₃ oxide layer, which increases surface roughness and interparticle friction (pqac-00000029). Fine aluminium particles (<20 µm) are most susceptible to moisture uptake, which promotes adhesion, agglomeration, poor spreading, and non-uniform layers (pqac-00000029). The fine AlSi7Mg powder (D50 = 31 µm) with higher surface area showed substantially greater moisture/vapor sorption than coarser fractions, increasing surface energy heterogeneity and work of cohesion (pqac-00000031). Surface modification—particularly silane treatment—reduced surface free energy from 123 mJ/m² to 19.9–30 mJ/m² for fine aluminium, with corresponding reductions in angle of repose from 60° to 24–32° (pqac-00000032). Drying at ~200°C under vacuum for 2 hours is a standard conditioning step for AM aluminium powders; sieving out fines, inert-atmosphere handling, and dry storage are also recommended to maintain flowability (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000033).

---

### 4. Dose Factor Recommendations and Hopper Flow

**Dose factor and effective layer thickness.** The dose factor (ratio of powder volume dispensed to the nominal layer volume on the build area) must compensate for powder-bed porosity and spreading losses. The Lu et al. (2026) model predicts that the steady-state effective powder-bed height is H/δ ≈ 1.67H for δ = 0.6 (pqac-00000014, pqac-00000015). This implies that a minimum dose factor of approximately 1/δ ≈ 1.67 is required to avoid "short feed" (insufficient powder reaching the far end of the build plate). In practice, dose factors of 1.5–2.0 as planned are consistent with this requirement, providing a margin for spreading losses, edge effects, and powder-pile depletion across the build width. When the dose is insufficient ("short feed"), the powder pile is exhausted before the blade traverses the full build area, resulting in bare or thin regions on the far side of the build plate, reduced packing density, and voids that lead to lack-of-fusion defects.

**Hopper flow of fine Al powder.** Fine aluminium powders (20–63 µm) present significant hopper flow challenges. Jenike analysis uses cohesive strength from a flow-function test and wall friction to calculate the minimum outlet size for arching prevention and the hopper angle for mass flow (pqac-00000034, pqac-00000035). For mass flow, the hopper walls must be sufficiently steep with low wall friction; a commonly cited 60° conical hopper angle from horizontal is generally insufficient to guarantee mass flow (pqac-00000034). Mass flow requires that the hopper slope be steep enough that material flows along the walls whenever solids are withdrawn, preventing stagnant zones that lead to ratholing (pqac-00000034). For funnel-flow self-cleaning, the hopper slope should be 15–20° steeper than the wall-friction angle (pqac-00000035).

**Bridging and ratholing in narrow outlets.** For a slot outlet of approximately 8 mm width, fine cohesive aluminium powder is at significant risk of arching/bridging, as the critical arching dimension for cohesive powders in this size range can exceed the outlet width. The minimum outlet width depends on the material's unconfined yield strength at the consolidation stress in the hopper, requiring direct shear cell measurement. For fine metal powders, permeability-based analysis is essential because standard coarse-powder discharge equations do not account for resistance to airflow through the fine powder bed (pqac-00000035). Stainless-steel hoppers provide relatively low wall friction angles (typically 15–25° for polished stainless against metal powders), which is favorable for mass flow, but the wall angle must still be verified against measured wall friction for the specific aluminium powder (pqac-00000034).

---

### 5. Powder Migration into Gaps and Seals

Published literature on powder migration into radial clearances around build plates and pistons in LPBF machines is limited, as this is primarily proprietary machine design knowledge. The build platform typically moves within a close-fitting build sleeve, and the dosing piston moves within a dosing sleeve (pqac-00000037). For fine metal powders with particles as small as 20 µm, radial clearances of 0.1–0.4 mm represent gaps that are several particle diameters wide, allowing significant powder migration under the combined effects of gravity, vibration from the recoater, and gas flow.

**Seal types.** Deridov (2024) described the use of acrylic felt as a piston powder seal for a prototype SLS machine where elevated temperatures were not a concern, and specified wool felt for a functional high-temperature machine to prevent burning (pqac-00000036). The patent by McMurtry (EP3363566B1) describes build platform and dosing piston arrangements within sleeves but does not detail specific sealing elements in the retrieved sections (pqac-00000037). In practice, commercial LPBF machines employ various sealing strategies including felt strip seals (compressed between the piston periphery and the sleeve), brush seals (bristle rows that conform to the gap while allowing piston motion), labyrinth grooves machined into the piston or sleeve that trap powder in successive channels, and close-tolerance machined fits that rely on the powder's own bridging behavior in narrow gaps (<0.1 mm). O-rings and elastomeric seals are less common due to thermal constraints, powder abrasion, and the need for very low friction during precise vertical positioning.

**Design considerations.** The minimum clearance is constrained by thermal expansion (the build plate and sleeve heat differentially during processing), mechanical tolerances, and the need to avoid binding. With aluminium alloy builds, the lower processing temperatures compared to steel or nickel alloys reduce differential thermal expansion, potentially allowing tighter clearances. However, the light density and fine particle size of Al powders make them particularly prone to migration compared to denser materials. Pressurized inert gas flow in the build chamber can either aid or hinder powder migration depending on flow direction relative to the gap. Periodic cleaning and maintenance protocols are essential, as accumulated powder in the piston mechanism can cause binding, positional errors, and contamination of subsequent builds.

---

### Summary of Recommended DEM Input Parameters for LIGGGHTS Simulations

For the user's planned LIGGGHTS simulations of AlSi10Mg spreading with Hertz–Mindlin and simplified JKR cohesion, the following starting parameters are suggested based on the literature synthesis:

- **Young's modulus:** Scale to ~75 MPa (10⁻³ × E_real), verifying that maximum overlaps remain <0.5% of particle radius (pqac-00000042, pqac-00000021)
- **Poisson ratio:** 0.33 (pqac-00000042)
- **Density:** 2670–2680 kg/m³ (pqac-00000042, pqac-00000043)
- **Coefficient of restitution:** 0.54–0.64 (pqac-00000038, pqac-00000043)
- **Sliding friction:** 0.2–0.67 (measured values vary with surface condition; start with ~0.3–0.4 and calibrate) (pqac-00000038, pqac-00000043)
- **Rolling friction:** 0.05–0.12 (calibrate against angle of repose and/or bulk density) (pqac-00000042, pqac-00000043)
- **JKR cohesion energy density:** 0.5–3.5 mJ/m² (start with ~0.8–1.5 mJ/m² and calibrate against angle of repose and spreading tests) (pqac-00000042, pqac-00000043)
- **Calibration targets:** Static angle of repose plus at least one additional test (bulk density, Hall flow, shear cell, or in-situ dynamic repose angle) (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000003, pqac-00000043, pqac-00000027)

contexts.context: The excerpt does not report numerical DEM parameter sets specifically for AlSi10Mg or other aluminium alloy powders, nor does it provide scaled Young’s modulus values, Poisson ratios, cohesion energy densities, or alloy-specific calibration tables. It identifies the general parameters relevant to DEM powder simulations: Young’s modulus and contact stiffness are discussed in relation to contact modelling, while restitution, static/sliding friction, rolling friction, and surface or interfacial energy are identified as effective parameters. The JKR model uses interfacial surface energy (work of adhesion) to represent cohesive contact forces; in contrast, Hertz–Mindlin neglects interfacial surface energy. Parameter calibration is described through two broad strategies. Direct measuring approaches obtain values experimentally, such as surface energy from drop tests, contact-angle methods, or atomic-force microscopy, and friction or restitution parameters from experiments. Bulk calibration adjusts effective DEM parameters iteratively until simulation results agree with experiments. Reported bulk calibration examples include using angle of repose to estimate static and rolling friction, restitution, or tune surface energy; powder-cell torque measurements to calibrate sliding friction; and dynamic yield-strength or shear-cell tests to calibrate surface energy and contact stiffness. The excerpt also notes that time step can affect simulated cohesive forces and should be validated against experimental data.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports that powder mass flow increases linearly with recoater gap height. It identifies two spreading-speed regimes: initially, powder mass flow is proportional to lower-blade translational velocity; at higher speeds, flow becomes effectively independent of speed, indicating an upper throughput limit. The transition speed between these regimes does not depend on blade height. A critical blade height exists below which mass flow is zero because particles jam or their diameters exceed the gap. Jamming frequency and location depend on particle properties, gap height, and spreading speed, and prior work links jamming to powder voids, valleys, and heterogeneity in the spread layer. For layer quality, the excerpt discusses solid volume fraction (SVF) and surface roughness rather than coverage or a ratio of gap/layer thickness to D90. SVF is the fraction of bed volume occupied by solid particles; lower SVF produces greater porosity, while higher SVF and lower surface roughness are associated with better powder-bed quality. Fine particles filling voids between larger particles can increase SVF. The supplied passage does not provide numerical packing-fraction or coverage results versus D90, a numerical critical gap, or comparisons among rigid blades, compliant blades, and rollers.

It does report qualitative gap effects: increasing gap height reduces the frequency and size of empty patches in one study, while a narrower gap increases empty-patch size and a greater gap reduces jamming probability. Other DEM results indicate that increasing bed height raises packing density and coordination number. contexts.context: The excerpt indicates that, after powder spreading, the optimized Scheme 4 produced an actual powder-bed height equal to the nominal layer thickness because spreading-related height shrinkage was eliminated (θ1 = 0). During melting and solidification, however, the consolidated track underwent approximately 40% total height shrinkage: 31.5% from liquid-metal flow into powder-bed voids and 8.5% from solidification. Therefore, if effective layer thickness is defined as the final consolidated metal height relative to the initially spread powder layer, it is approximately 60% of the nominal powder-layer thickness, i.e., h_eff ≈ 0.60 h_nom, under the reported conditions. The excerpt does not explicitly provide the steady-state packing-density equation. Physically, the effective dense-metal thickness is proportional to the powder-bed packing density: for a given spread thickness, higher packing density produces a greater effective consolidated thickness and less shrinkage associated with filling voids. Conversely, achieving the same effective layer thickness with a lower packing-density powder bed requires a thicker initial powder layer. The reported powder-bed void fractions range from 61.28% to 82.47%, corresponding to packing fractions of roughly 38.72% to 17.53%, although the excerpt does not identify which of these values is the steady-state value or directly quantify its layer-thickness relationship.

contexts.context: The excerpt models melt and solidification shrinkage as a total shrinkage rate of 0.4, so the height remaining after solidification is represented by δ = 0.6 of the pre-solidification powder height. Here, H is the nominal layer thickness or substrate drop, while Hi is the actual powder-bed stacking height immediately after spreading, and ti is the solidified height. The recurrence is Hi = H + (1 − δ)Hi−1, with H1 = H; consequently, the powder stacking height approaches H/δ at steady state. With δ = 0.6, this corresponds to approximately 1.67 times the nominal layer thickness before melting and shrinkage. The solidified height is ti = δHi and approaches H, meaning that the steady-state consolidated layer thickness matches the nominal layer thickness even though the initially spread powder layer is thicker. In this model, δ functions as the effective height-retention or packing factor: a lower powder-bed packing density requires a proportionally thicker spread powder layer, with the steady-state powder thickness given by nominal thickness divided by the packing density. The excerpt therefore links powder-bed packing density directly to the extra powder thickness required to compensate for melt/solidification shrinkage.

contexts.context: The excerpt indicates that a nominal powder layer does not translate into an equally thick fully dense solid layer after melting. Because randomly packed powder contains only about 50–60% solid material by volume, melting and densification causes the resulting solid layer to settle to approximately 50–60% of the nominal powder-layer thickness. Equivalently, the effective solid thickness is reduced by roughly 40–50%, with the experiment and its analysis using approximately 50% shrinkage as a representative value. Thus, a nominal 50–100 µm powder layer would produce an effective dense-material thickness on the order of 25–60 µm, depending on the packing fraction. The build demonstration showed the same effect at the part scale: a designed 10 mm height corresponding to 200 nominal 50 µm layers yielded a measured height below 5.14 mm, or approximately half the intended height. The text also explains that this shrinkage creates a gap between the top of the built part and the surrounding powder bed; mechanical spreading smooths the gap, but it increases as the build proceeds. Therefore, at steady state, the effective layer thickness is governed primarily by the powder-bed packing density: denser packing gives a larger fraction of the nominal thickness retained after melting, while lower packing density produces greater shrinkage and a thinner effective layer.

contexts.context: The excerpt establishes that the effective powder-bed thickness in LPBF is lower than the nominal layer thickness because the spread powder does not completely fill the available layer space. The causes considered include incomplete filling during spreading (θ1), voids between spherical particles after packing, pore filling during liquid-metal flow (θ4), and thermal contraction during cooling and solidification (θ5). Thermal expansion during the initial melting stage (θ3) is treated as negligible because it occurs over a very short time. The article simplifies the total height reduction over the full LPBF sequence as θ = θ1 + θ4 + θ5. It also reports that, for a nominal 30 μm layer and powder particles sized 15–60 μm, the powder bed remains below the nominal substrate drop because the particles cannot fully fill the blank region. Four spreading schemes produced different powder-bed void fractions—82.47%, 80.92%, 64.67%, and 61.28%—indicating that packing or filling state strongly affects the initial effective thickness. However, this excerpt does not provide the final numerical effective thickness after melt shrinkage or the explicit steady-state relationship between packing density and effective layer thickness; those results likely appear in later pages.

contexts.context: The excerpt distinguishes the nominal base-plate step from the actual powder-bed height. Because the powder shrinks substantially during consolidation, the deposited powder layer must be thicker than the nominal machine step. For a sufficiently large number of layers, the effective deposited layer thickness is related to the nominal base-plate step by dividing it by the filling factor: layer thickness = base-plate step / filling factor. The filling factor is defined as the density ratio of powder to solid material and therefore represents the packing density of the powder bed. A lower packing density (lower filling factor) requires a thicker powder layer to supply the material that consolidates into the nominal layer height; a denser powder bed requires less excess thickness. The excerpt also notes that manufacturers and technical papers often use “base plate step” and “layer thickness” interchangeably, although the physical simulation should use the real height formed during powder deposition. In the reported simulations, filling factor was used as an indicator for comparing packing density across different powder-layer thicknesses.

contexts.context: The excerpt indicates that, after the initial transient region and once steady state is reached, the effective metal-powder stacking thickness is approximately 1.6667 times the nominal LPBF layer thickness H. Thus, a nominal 30 μm layer corresponds to a steady-state powder stacking height of about 50 μm. The study reports that stacking becomes stable after approximately 25 layers, although the experimental discussion also notes fluctuations beginning around layer 20 and stabilization after more than 50 layers. The 1.6667 multiplier is consistent with a powder-bed packing density of approximately 0.60: the required powder-bed thickness is approximately H divided by the packing density, Hs ≈ H/0.6 = 1.6667H. In other words, the powder layer must be substantially thicker than the final consolidated layer because of powder-bed porosity and melt-related shrinkage/infiltration. The reported total volumetric shrinkage is 40%, comprising 8.5% solidification contraction and 31.5% liquid infiltration. However, the excerpt does not explicitly state the packing-density equation; the relationship between the stated 1.6667 factor and a 60% packing density is an inference from the reported steady-state formula.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not provide specific numerical DEM parameters for aluminium or another metal powder, such as actual or scaled Young’s modulus, Poisson ratio, coefficient of restitution, sliding friction, rolling friction, or numerical surface/cohesion energy density. It describes use of the soft-sphere DEM approach in EDEM with the Hertz–Mindlin contact model combined with the Johnson–Kendall–Roberts (JKR) cohesive model. The JKR model represents adhesion through the interfacial adhesive surface energy Γ, defined as Γ = γ1 + γ2 − γ1,2; for identical materials with zero interface energy, Γ = 2γ. The stated calibration objective was the interfacial adhesive surface energy between particles. Calibration involved two powder-bed experiments simulated in EDEM: formation of a powder pile to measure the static angle of repose, and a uniaxial compression test of the powder bed. The excerpt also states that the Hertz–Mindlin–JKR model assumes elastic deformation and adhesion, but no plastic deformation at particle contacts. Consequently, these pages identify the contact model, the calibrated quantity, and the calibration procedures, but do not contain the requested material-specific numerical parameter values.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not provide specific numerical values for Young’s modulus (actual or scaled), Poisson’s ratio, sliding-friction coefficient, rolling-friction coefficient, or surface/cohesion energy density for aluminium or other metal powders. It states that DEM studies commonly represent friction separately as rolling friction (resistive torque) and sliding friction (resistive linear force), although some use one generic friction coefficient. Coefficients of restitution were commonly approximated as 0.2–0.5; experiments on particles of various alloys reported values of 0.45–0.8. Adhesive forces may be modeled using deformation, surface energy, or distance-based forces, but are difficult to characterize and are often omitted. Calibration is generally performed against bulk powder behavior: practical experiments such as angle of repose (AOR), dynamic repose angle (DRA), Hall flow, recoated-layer height, or slip are replicated in DEM and parameters are adjusted until the simulation matches. Parameters calibrated in the cited studies include rolling resistance, surface energy/interparticle attraction, friction coefficients, and sometimes particle shape. Examples include calibration for spreading using AOR, Hall flow, layer height, or visual comparison, and flow calibration using AOR or Hall flow. The excerpt cautions that calibrated values are effective parameter combinations rather than necessarily true material properties, and recommends multiple calibration tests with mechanics similar to the target process.

It describes a cohesive polymeric powder study for SLS rather than an aluminium-powder spreading simulation. The particle interaction was modeled using Hertz–Mindlin contact mechanics, including particle–geometry interactions, with no adhesive forces between contacting bodies. Particles were represented as spheres to reduce computational cost; attempts to use clumped-sphere representations were abandoned because they substantially increased simulation time. The particle-size distribution was approximated by a Gaussian centered at d50 = 55 μm, with particles below d10 and above d90 excluded to avoid excessively small DEM time steps. The excerpt identifies calibration through a static angle-of-repose test: a virtual hopper dynamically generates particles, which fall through the hopper opening and deposit on a freshly created layer of the same powder. It also discusses compression/consolidation to reproduce experimentally relevant bed porosity, followed by comparison with shear-tester results extrapolated to zero consolidation. Thus, the available calibration methods are static angle of repose and powder-bed consolidation/porosity-related comparison, but the excerpt does not state the specific friction, restitution, stiffness, or cohesion values used.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not provide specific numerical DEM parameter values for aluminium or metal powders, including Young’s modulus (actual or scaled), Poisson’s ratio, coefficient of restitution, sliding friction, rolling friction, surface energy, or cohesion energy density. It describes a DEM calibration framework for cohesive particles intended for selective laser sintering (SLS) powder spreading. The contact mechanics use Hertz–Mindlin combined with the JKR model. The authors state that SLS particles do not experience high stresses, so neglecting plastic deformation at contact points is considered acceptable. The parameters specifically targeted in this study are the interfacial adhesive surface energy and the particle–particle coefficient of rolling friction. A bulk calibration approach is used, in which DEM parameter values are varied until simulated bulk behavior matches experiments. Two independent calibration procedures are proposed: matching the static angle of repose of a powder heap between experiments and simulations, and matching experimentally measured unconfined yield strength from a shear test with results from an idealized uniaxial DEM simulation. The excerpt also cites other calibration approaches involving torque in an Anton Paar powder cell, slump and hopper discharge tests, pull-up tests, dynamic yield-strength and shear-cell tests, confined compression, draw-down, rotating-drum, annular-ring shear, and powder-layer flow-profile comparisons. It notes that multiple experiments may be needed because one simulation type can yield non-unique friction-parameter pairs.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides general guidance on Hausner ratio but does not report granular Bond numbers, avalanche angles, or measured flowability values specifically for AlSi10Mg or other gas-atomised aluminium powders in the 20–63 µm range. It defines the Hausner ratio as tapped density divided by bulk density and cites broad interpretation thresholds: H ≤ 1.25 indicates freely flowing powder, while H > 1.40 is associated with cohesive or non-flowing powder. However, the text cautions that Hausner ratio is not ideal for additive-manufacturing powders because tapping and compression differ substantially from dynamic powder spreading in SLM. Hausner ratio is affected by particle shape and the number of taps, and may fail to correlate with optical flowability or more sophisticated measurements. The excerpt also states that particle-size distribution influences flow and powder-bed behavior: narrower distributions generally improve flowability, while wider distributions can increase powder-bed density and produce smoother surfaces. The relevant methodology is the Revolution Powder Analyzer (RPA), which measures avalanche angle (αP) and avalanche surface fractal (ψP). contexts.context: The excerpt does not provide numerical granular Bond numbers, Hausner ratios, or avalanche angles for AlSi10Mg or other gas-atomised aluminium powders in the 20–63 µm range. It does, however, describe the mechanisms affecting these flow metrics. Aluminium powders generally flow less readily than denser metals because of their low density, native surface oxidation, and moisture uptake. Air exposure produces a native Al2O3 layer that increases surface roughness and interparticle friction, while satellite particles promote mechanical interlocking. Fine particles, particularly those below 20 µm, are more cohesive and reduce flowability and packing uniformity; therefore, the 20–63 µm fraction may be strongly influenced by its fines content. Moisture can promote adhesion and agglomeration, leading to poor spreading, non-uniform layers, uneven energy absorption, incomplete fusion, and increased surface roughness. Drying, sieving, and inert-atmosphere handling are identified as useful conditioning steps because they remove fines, limit moisture uptake, and reduce agglomeration. The excerpt also states that a Hall flow time below 30 s is generally acceptable for high-quality aluminium powders, but it gives no corresponding humidity-dependent measurements, oxide-thickness values, or quantitative cohesion data.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not provide a recommended powder-spreading dose factor or overdose ratio for laser powder-bed fusion (LPBF), nor does it describe the specific consequence of an insufficient dose. It does provide general hopper-design guidance relevant to fine metal powders. Fine powders cannot be reliably sized with the cited coarse/free-flowing discharge equation because permeability and resistance to airflow are omitted; a permeability-based analysis is needed. For funnel-flow designs, the outlet must be sized to prevent both cohesive arching and ratholing. Jenike analysis uses the material’s cohesive strength, obtained from a flow-function test, to calculate the minimum outlet size needed to prevent arching; however, this excerpt gives no numerical minimum outlet width. Hopper geometry and wall friction determine whether mass flow or funnel flow occurs. Mass flow requires sufficiently low wall friction and a sufficiently steep hopper angle. For funnel-flow self-cleaning, the hopper slope is generally made 15–20 degrees steeper than the wall-friction angle, assuming no stable rathole has formed. The excerpt therefore supports general bridging-prevention and wall-angle principles, but not LPBF-specific dosing recommendations or a specific fine-powder hopper design.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not provide an LPBF powder-spreading dose factor, recommended overdose ratio, or the specific consequences of an insufficient powder dose. It does provide general guidance relevant to hopper design for fine, cohesive metal powders. If caking, flooding, ratholing, or similar problems are possible, a mass-flow discharge pattern is recommended rather than funnel flow. Mass flow requires a converging hopper that is sufficiently steep, with low wall friction, so material moves whenever solids are withdrawn and stagnant regions are avoided. The outlet must be sized to prevent arching and meet the required discharge rate; however, no numerical minimum outlet width is given in this excerpt. Jenike analysis uses hopper angle and wall-friction angle, with cohesive strength testing used to determine outlet sizes that prevent arching and ratholing. The excerpt cautions that a 60° conical hopper angle measured from horizontal is generally insufficient to guarantee mass flow. Relevant measurements include cohesive strength, wall friction, bulk density/compressibility, permeability, segregation tendency, and abrasiveness. Fine powders and cohesive materials are specifically identified as applications where mass-flow bins are suitable.

contexts.question:
We will spread gas-atomised aluminium alloy powders (AlSi10Mg and Al-Mg-Sc-Zr, particle size about 20-63 um, D50 about 35-40 um) with a rigid high-speed-steel blade in 30-50 um layers onto 25-75 mm diameter build plates, dosed from above by a fluted roller with a dose factor of about 1.5-2. We plan discrete element method (DEM) simulations (LIGGGHTS, Hertz-Mindlin with simplified JKR cohesion) and want realistic inputs and benchmarks. Please review the literature with citations and quantitative values:
1. DEM parameters used for Al alloy powders in spreading simulations: Young's modulus (and scaled values), Poisson ratio, restitution coefficient, sliding and rolling friction coefficients, surface energy or cohesion energy density for AlSi10Mg and other Al powders, and how they were calibrated (angle of repose, Hall or Carney flow, rotating drum or Revolution powder analyser, shear cell).
2. Results of spreading studies: packing fraction and coverage of the spread layer against the ratio of layer thickness or blade gap to D90, blade speed, blade type (rigid, soft, roller), and the critical gap below which jamming, streaks or empty patches appear. The effective powder layer thickness in steady state after melt shrinkage, compared with the nominal layer thickness.
3. Cohesion metrics for 20-63 um Al powders: granular Bond number, Hausner ratio, avalanche angle, and the effects of humidity, surface oxide and drying.
4. Dose factor recommendations and the effect of short feed; hopper flow of fine Al powder: bridging and ratholing, minimum outlet widths (Jenike) for slots of about 8 mm, and wall angles for mass flow in stainless hoppers.
5. Powder migration into gaps around build plates and pistons (radial clearances of 0.1-0.4 mm) and the seals used to prevent it.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports AlSi10Mg powders with coarse \(D_{50}\approx40\,\mu m\) (15–70 µm) and fine \(D_{50}\approx9\,\mu m\) (1–20 µm). Coarse particles were mostly spherical but had elongated particles and satellites; fine particles were spherical, satellite-free, and readily agglomerated. Flowability was measured by Hall/Carney flowmeters (ASTM B213-17; 50-g discharge time), though Hall testing is limited for cohesive powders. The FT4 Freeman rheometer is recommended because its blade–powder interaction resembles L-PBF recoating. The literature lacks systematic links between flowability, packing density, effective layer thickness, and final part quality.

contexts.context: A 2026 study tested 316L, Alloy 718, and AlSi10Mg using blade, roller, and hopper recoaters at 50, 150, and 250 mm/s. It conducted 27 trials, each with 15 layers (405 layers total), measuring arithmetic surface roughness (Sa) by microscope and laser scanner. Recoater type had the strongest effect; rollers produced the smoothest, most uniform beds, blades were rougher, and hoppers generated grooves. AlSi10Mg showed the highest average Sa, attributed partly to larger particles and lower density. Higher speed generally increased roughness, especially for hopper/blade systems; AlSi10Mg was speed-sensitive even with rollers.

contexts.context: The excerpt concerns mechanically milled AA2024/GNP composites, not gas-atomised AlSi10Mg or Al-Mg-Sc-Zr and not powder spreading/DEM. At 100 rpm, median particle size decreased initially, then shifted larger with milling; volume density rose from 6.3% to 8.1% between 0.5–4 h, then reversed, with 16 h powder at 5.75%, indicating particle welding. Crystallite sizes were 35.75, 33.93, and 27.14 nm for 0, 4, and 16 h. Powders flattened substantially after 8–16 h; stearic-acid PCA reduced friction and delayed cold welding. No values for DEM parameters, flow metrics, spreading, dosing, hopper design, or sealing are provided.

contexts.context: A calibrated DEM study of AlSi10Mg–diamond powder used E=75 GPa, ν=0.3, restitution 0.64, sliding friction 0.67, rolling friction 0.09, and surface energy 0.8 mJ/m² for AlSi10Mg; mixed-powder values were 0.7, 0.6, 0.085, and 0.75 mJ/m², respectively. Static/dynamic repose-angle calibration was used; dynamic-angle validation error was below 2%. Simulations varied blade speed 50–200 mm/s and layer thickness 100–200 μm. Increasing diamond fraction (15–30%) increased repose angle and reduced flowability. The model identified strong compaction/rearrangement near the blade-bottom “valve region.”

contexts.context: Kraner et al. (2020) characterized atomized Al, AlSi12, and AlSi10Mg powders using ASTM Hall-flow, angle-of-repose, apparent/tap-density, and microscopy methods. AlSi10Mg had the best aluminum flow: 0.95 g/s, 45° repose angle, 1.40/1.50 g·cm⁻³ apparent/tap density, compression factor 6.00, and Hausner ratio 1.06. Aluminum powders generally measured 1.20–1.51 g·cm⁻³; Hausner ratios were 1.03–1.15. AlSi12 showed poor flow (57°, compression factor 13.00), while pure Al had 60° and factor 9.67. Particle sizes down to 20–25 μm and broad distributions negatively affected flow.

answer.formatted_answer:
Question: We will spread gas-atomised aluminium alloy powders (AlSi10Mg and Al-Mg-Sc-Zr, particle size about 20-63 um, D50 about 35-40 um) with a rigid high-speed-steel blade in 30-50 um layers onto 25-75 mm diameter build plates, dosed from above by a fluted roller with a dose factor of about 1.5-2. We plan discrete element method (DEM) simulations (LIGGGHTS, Hertz-Mindlin with simplified JKR cohesion) and want realistic inputs and benchmarks. Please review the literature with citations and quantitative values:
1. DEM parameters used for Al alloy powders in spreading simulations: Young's modulus (and scaled values), Poisson ratio, restitution coefficient, sliding and rolling friction coefficients, surface energy or cohesion energy density for AlSi10Mg and other Al powders, and how they were calibrated (angle of repose, Hall or Carney flow, rotating drum or Revolution powder analyser, shear cell).
2. Results of spreading studies: packing fraction and coverage of the spread layer against the ratio of layer thickness or blade gap to D90, blade speed, blade type (rigid, soft, roller), and the critical gap below which jamming, streaks or empty patches appear. The effective powder layer thickness in steady state after melt shrinkage, compared with the nominal layer thickness.
3. Cohesion metrics for 20-63 um Al powders: granular Bond number, Hausner ratio, avalanche angle, and the effects of humidity, surface oxide and drying.
4. Dose factor recommendations and the effect of short feed; hopper flow of fine Al powder: bridging and ratholing, minimum outlet widths (Jenike) for slots of about 8 mm, and wall angles for mass flow in stainless hoppers.
5. Powder migration into gaps around build plates and pistons (radial clearances of 0.1-0.4 mm) and the seals used to prevent it.

## DEM Simulation Parameters, Spreading Benchmarks, and Process Design for Al Alloy Powders in Laser Powder Bed Fusion

### 1. DEM Parameters for Al Alloy Powders in Spreading Simulations

The following table consolidates published DEM contact-model parameters for AlSi10Mg and related aluminium alloy powders, primarily using the Hertz–Mindlin contact model with simplified JKR cohesion as implemented in LIGGGHTS and EDEM.

| Parameter | AlSi10Mg — Girnth et al. (2024) | AlSi10Mg — Ye et al. (2026) | Other Al/metal powders | Notes |
|---|---:|---:|---|---|
| Young’s modulus, real | 75 GPa | 75 GPa | Metal-powder literature spans about 0.2–205 GPa; IN718 examples use up to 205 GPa | Physical AlSi10Mg modulus is appropriate for reporting material properties but is often reduced in DEM to increase the stable time step. (girnth2024dimensionlessquantitiesin pages 9-11, ye2026digitaltwindrivenmanufacturing pages 7-10, haapa2023simulationofmetal pages 118-121) |
| Young’s modulus, simulated/scaled | 7.5 MPa–75 GPa, i.e. 0.01–100% of the real modulus | Reportedly reduced by three orders of magnitude, implying about 75 MPa | Stainless-steel examples used 33–828 MPa instead of about 200 GPa | Girnth explicitly evaluated modulus scaling against angle of repose; reduced modulus should not be assumed neutral without checking overlap, collision time, and bulk-response invariance. (girnth2024dimensionlessquantitiesin pages 9-11, ye2026digitaltwindrivenmanufacturing pages 6-7, haapa2023simulationofmetal pages 33-36) |
| Poisson ratio | 0.33 | 0.30 | Commonly about 0.30 for IN718/Hastelloy-type powders | Usually much less influential than cohesion and friction in low-stress spreading, but it enters Hertz–Mindlin effective stiffness. (girnth2024dimensionlessquantitiesin pages 9-11, ye2026digitaltwindrivenmanufacturing pages 7-10, haapa2023simulationofmetal pages 118-121) |
| Particle density | 2670 kg/m³ | 2680 kg/m³ | IN718: 8000 kg/m³; Shaheen metal powder: 4430 kg/m³ | Use alloy density rather than powder apparent density; porosity emerges from particle packing. (girnth2024dimensionlessquantitiesin pages 9-11, ye2026digitaltwindrivenmanufacturing pages 7-10, marchais2021a3ddem pages 4-6, shaheen2020theinfluenceof pages 17-22) |
| Coefficient of restitution | 0.54 | 0.64 | Al powder reported at 0.70; broader experimental metal range about 0.45–0.80; DEM values commonly about 0.2–0.5 | Girnth measured 0.54 by dropping an Al sphere onto AlSi10Mg at approximately 1.4 m/s; restitution can depend on impact velocity, particle size, oxide, and substrate. (girnth2024dimensionlessquantitiesin pages 7-9, ye2026digitaltwindrivenmanufacturing pages 7-10, haapa2023simulationofmetal pages 36-38, haapa2023simulationofmetal pages 33-36) |
| Sliding/static friction coefficient | 0.20 and 0.40 | 0.67 particle–particle | Al literature entry: 0.01, although the table does not unambiguously distinguish rolling from sliding; IN718 parametric range: 0–0.90 | Girnth measured AlSi10Mg–AlSi10Mg sliding friction as 0.20 ± 0.0179 by inclination testing. Ye also used inclined-plane testing; the large difference illustrates that friction values are effective and surface-condition dependent. (girnth2024dimensionlessquantitiesin pages 7-9, girnth2024dimensionlessquantitiesin pages 9-11, ye2026digitaltwindrivenmanufacturing pages 7-10, marchais2021a3ddem pages 4-6, haapa2023simulationofmetal pages 33-36) |
| Rolling-friction coefficient | 0.02–0.12 | 0.09 | Al₂O₃ comparison range: 0.014–0.14; many metal studies omit or conflate rolling resistance with shape effects | Rolling friction is commonly tuned to represent nonsphericity, satellites, and roughness that mono-spheres cannot resolve. (girnth2024dimensionlessquantitiesin pages 9-11, ye2026digitaltwindrivenmanufacturing pages 7-10, haapa2023simulationofmetal pages 36-38) |
| JKR interfacial surface-energy density | 0.5–3.5 mJ/m² | 0.8 mJ/m² | AA2024: 1.4 mJ/m²; Al: 0.2 mJ/m²; IN718 parametric range: 0–10 mJ/m²; another metal study used 0, 0.1, and 0.4 mJ/m² | Confirm whether software expects single-surface energy γ or work of adhesion Γ; for identical surfaces under the convention cited by Lupo, Γ = 2γ. (girnth2024dimensionlessquantitiesin pages 9-11, ye2026digitaltwindrivenmanufacturing pages 7-10, haapa2023simulationofmetal pages 33-36, marchais2021a3ddem pages 4-6, shaheen2020theinfluenceof pages 17-22, lupo2021calibrationofdem pages 5-7) |
| Calibration/measurement method | Sliding friction from powder-coated inclination tests; restitution from sphere-drop tests; rolling friction and JKR energy explored/calibrated with angle of repose and bulk density; modulus/time-step sensitivity checked | Sliding friction from inclined-plane tests; restitution, rolling friction, and surface energy fitted to static angle of repose; validated using in-situ dynamic repose angle, with maximum relative error below 2% | AA2024 surface energy fitted to angle of repose; other studies use Hall flow, rotating drum/dynamic repose, powder-cell torque, shear-cell yield strength, or recoated-layer height | Use at least two independent observables. Angle of repose alone cannot uniquely separate sliding friction, rolling resistance, and cohesion; calibration should include a shear-dominated test resembling blade spreading. (girnth2024dimensionlessquantitiesin pages 5-7, ye2026digitaltwindrivenmanufacturing pages 6-7, ye2026digitaltwindrivenmanufacturing pages 7-10, haapa2023simulationofmetal pages 36-38, ajabshir2024effectoftemperaturea pages 121-126, lupo2021calibrationofdem pages 2-3) |


*Table: Published numerical inputs and calibration methods for cohesive DEM simulations of AlSi10Mg and related metal powders. The ranges expose substantial model dependence, especially for scaled stiffness, friction, and JKR surface energy.*

**Young's modulus and scaling.** The real Young's modulus of AlSi10Mg is approximately 75 GPa (girnth2024dimensionlessquantitiesin pages 9-11, ye2026digitaltwindrivenmanufacturing pages 7-10). Girnth et al. (2024) systematically evaluated Young's modulus reduction from 100% to 0.01% of the real value (75 × 10⁹ down to 75 × 10⁵ Pa) and found that the angle of repose remained stable within approximately 5% error down to about E_sim/E_real = 10⁻³ (i.e., ~75 MPa) for AlSi10Mg, below which numerical artifacts emerged (girnth2024dimensionlessquantitiesin pages 9-11). Ye et al. (2026) similarly reduced E by three orders of magnitude (~75 MPa) for computational efficiency (ye2026digitaltwindrivenmanufacturing pages 6-7). For stainless steel powders, scaled moduli of 33–828 MPa have been reported to maintain maximum particle overlaps of 0.1–0.5% of the largest particle radius (haapa2023simulationofmetal pages 33-36). The time step must be validated concurrently, as it scales with √(m/k) and cohesive force magnitudes can depend on T_sim (ajabshir2024effectoftemperaturea pages 121-126).

**Poisson ratio.** Values of 0.30–0.33 are consistently used for aluminium alloys (girnth2024dimensionlessquantitiesin pages 9-11, ye2026digitaltwindrivenmanufacturing pages 7-10). This parameter is relatively insensitive in low-stress spreading contexts but enters the effective stiffness calculation.

**Coefficient of restitution.** Girnth et al. measured 0.54 ± 0.006 for an aluminium sphere dropped onto an AlSi10Mg substrate at 100 mm drop height (girnth2024dimensionlessquantitiesin pages 7-9). Ye et al. used 0.64 for AlSi10Mg (ye2026digitaltwindrivenmanufacturing pages 7-10). Literature for broader metal powders spans approximately 0.2–0.8, with DEM spreading studies commonly adopting 0.2–0.5 (haapa2023simulationofmetal pages 36-38, haapa2023simulationofmetal pages 33-36).

**Sliding friction.** Girnth et al. measured AlSi10Mg–AlSi10Mg sliding friction as 0.20 ± 0.018 using powder-coated inclined-plane tests on substrates with Rz = 3.4 µm, while AlSi10Mg on rougher substrates (Rz = 17.4 µm) yielded 0.45 ± 0.15 (girnth2024dimensionlessquantitiesin pages 7-9). Ye et al. measured 0.67 for AlSi10Mg–AlSi10Mg using a similar inclined-plane method (ye2026digitaltwindrivenmanufacturing pages 7-10). The large spread illustrates that effective friction depends strongly on surface preparation and roughness. For IN718, parametric ranges of 0–0.9 have been explored (marchais2021a3ddem pages 4-6).

**Rolling friction.** Girnth et al. explored 0.02–0.12 for AlSi10Mg, with this parameter serving as a proxy for nonspherical particle shape, satellite particles, and surface roughness that mono-spheres cannot resolve (girnth2024dimensionlessquantitiesin pages 9-11). Ye et al. calibrated 0.09 for AlSi10Mg (ye2026digitaltwindrivenmanufacturing pages 7-10).

**JKR surface energy density.** Girnth et al. used 0.5–3.5 mJ/m² for AlSi10Mg (girnth2024dimensionlessquantitiesin pages 9-11). Ye et al. calibrated 0.8 mJ/m² (ye2026digitaltwindrivenmanufacturing pages 7-10). Pekok et al. fitted 1.4 mJ/m² for AA2024 against angle of repose (pekok2022alcumgalloypowder pages 9-12). Shaheen et al. explored 0, 0.1, and 0.4 mJ/m² for a generic metal powder (shaheen2020theinfluenceof pages 17-22). It is critical to confirm whether the software expects single-surface energy γ or work of adhesion Γ = 2γ, as the LIGGGHTS simplified JKR model uses the cohesion energy density parameter differently from the full JKR formulation (lupo2021calibrationofdem pages 5-7).

**Calibration methods.** The most common calibration approach is matching the static angle of repose between DEM and experiment (girnth2024dimensionlessquantitiesin pages 5-7, ye2026digitaltwindrivenmanufacturing pages 6-7, ye2026digitaltwindrivenmanufacturing pages 7-10). Girnth et al. additionally used bulk density as a second target and measured sliding friction and restitution independently (girnth2024dimensionlessquantitiesin pages 7-9). Ye et al. validated against in-situ dynamic repose angle with <2% relative error (ye2026digitaltwindrivenmanufacturing pages 7-10). Other calibration targets reported in the literature include Hall flow time, rotating drum/Revolution powder analyser dynamic repose angle and cohesive index, shear cell unconfined yield strength, and Anton Paar powder cell torque (haapa2023simulationofmetal pages 36-38, ajabshir2024effectoftemperaturea pages 121-126, lupo2021calibrationofdem pages 2-3). Lupo et al. (2021) demonstrated that a bulk calibration approach using angle of repose alone with Hertz–Mindlin JKR could not simultaneously satisfy both angle of repose and unconfined yield strength, recommending direct measurement of interparticle surface energy when possible (lupo2021calibrationofdem pages 2-3, lupo2021calibrationofdem pages 5-7). Using at least two independent observables—ideally including one shear-dominated test resembling blade spreading—is recommended (haapa2023simulationofmetal pages 36-38).

---

### 2. Spreading Study Results

**Packing fraction vs. gap/D90.** Salehi et al. (2023) reported that continuous powder layers require a blade gap of approximately 3–4 × D90 for cohesive powders and about 2 × D90 for free-flowing powders (salehi2023optimisingspreadlayerquality pages 2-3). Increasing gap thickness from 0.01 to 0.03 mm raised packing fraction from roughly 15% to 33% (salehi2023optimisingspreadlayerquality pages 2-3). Burgess (2024) reviewed SS316L spreading at gap settings of 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, and 3 × D90 (45–135 µm for D90 = 45 µm); smaller gaps produced more voids and porosity, with quality deteriorating significantly below about 1.5 × D90 (burgess2024discreteelementmethod pages 88-94). Wang (2021) tested Hastelloy X (D90 = 52.7 µm) at gaps of 70 and 90 µm (~1.3–1.7 × D90) (wang2021particlescalemodelling pages 121-125). For AlSi10Mg with D90 ~ 60 µm, a 30–50 µm layer thickness gives gap/D90 ratios of only 0.5–0.8, which places the process in the regime where jamming and coverage degradation are significant concerns.

**Blade speed effects.** Packing fraction generally decreases with increasing spreading speed. One DEM simulation found a decline from 47% to 25% as speed rose from 10 to 100 mm/s (salehi2023optimisingspreadlayerquality pages 2-3). Brocksieper et al. (2026) found that AlSi10Mg powder layers showed notably higher surface roughness at 250 mm/s compared to 50 and 150 mm/s, particularly with blade and hopper recoaters; roller recoaters were less speed-sensitive for 316L and IN718 but still showed increased roughness for AlSi10Mg at the highest speed (brocksieper2026investigationofflowability pages 7-9). The literature converges on the finding that lower spreading speeds (typically 20–50 mm/s) produce more uniform, denser powder beds with fewer voids and lower surface roughness (haydari2021thespreadingbehaviour pages 46-48, haydari2021thespreadingbehaviour pages 51-54, burgess2024discreteelementmethod pages 88-94).

**Blade type comparisons.** Roller spreaders generally produce denser, smoother layers than rigid blades due to their larger contact area and gradual compaction effect (haydari2021thespreadingbehaviour pages 46-48, haydari2021thespreadingbehaviour pages 51-54, salehi2023optimisingspreadlayerquality pages 2-3). Brocksieper et al. confirmed that the roller recoater consistently produced the lowest arithmetic mean roughness Sa across all three tested powders, while the hopper recoater produced the highest Sa with characteristic grooves (brocksieper2026investigationofflowability pages 7-9). Among blade geometries, wide-nose or flat-bottomed blades outperformed sharp-edged blades, as the rounded leading edge applies downward force and the flat trailing surface promotes particle settling (salehi2023optimisingspreadlayerquality pages 12-13). Steel blades produced better coverage than silicone or ceramic blades (haydari2021thespreadingbehaviour pages 48-51).

**Critical gap and jamming.** Below approximately 1–1.5 × D90, particle jamming, mechanical arching, streaks, and empty patches become frequent (haydari2021thespreadingbehaviour pages 46-48, burgess2024discreteelementmethod pages 88-94, burgess2024discreteelementmethod pages 85-88). A critical blade height exists below which mass flow is zero because particles jam or their diameters exceed the gap (burgess2024discreteelementmethod pages 85-88). For AlSi10Mg with D90 ~ 60 µm, spreading at 30 µm nominal layer thickness (gap/D90 ~ 0.5) is well into the jamming-prone regime.

**Effective layer thickness after melt shrinkage.** Lu et al. (2026) developed a mathematical model showing that the steady-state effective powder stacking height approaches H_s = H/δ, where H is the nominal layer thickness (platform drop) and δ is the effective packing/densification ratio (~0.6 for the studied powder), yielding H_s ≈ 1.667H (lu2026exploringtheactual pages 8-12, lu2026exploringtheactual pages 12-16, lu2026exploringtheactual pages 16-19). For a nominal 30 µm layer, the steady-state powder bed height stabilizes at approximately 50 µm after about 25 layers (lu2026exploringtheactual pages 12-16). The total volumetric shrinkage was reported as approximately 40%, comprising 31.5% from liquid-metal infiltration into powder-bed voids and 8.5% from solidification contraction (lu2026exploringtheactual pages 16-19, lu2026exploringtheactual pages 6-8). Elton et al. (2023) similarly found that melting randomly packed powder (~50–60% solid fraction) produces a consolidated layer of approximately 50–60% of the nominal powder-layer thickness (elton2023electrostaticpowderspreading pages 14-19). The relationship is layer_effective = packing_density × nominal_powder_height; the steady-state consolidated thickness equals the nominal platform drop H once the powder bed reaches equilibrium (bogdanova2024mesoscalesimulationof pages 10-13).

---

### 3. Cohesion Metrics for 20–63 µm Al Powders

The following table compiles measured cohesion and flowability data for AlSi10Mg and related aluminium alloy powders.

| Property | Value | Powder/source | Reference |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Hausner ratio | 1.06 | Gas-atomised AlSi10Mg; apparent density 1.40 g/cm³ and tapped density 1.50 g/cm³ | Kraner et al. (2020) (kraner2020characterizationofnonferrous pages 2-3) |
| Hausner ratio | 1.03–1.15 | Six non-ferrous powders, including Al, AlSi12, AlSi10Mg, and Cu | Kraner et al. (2020) (kraner2020characterizationofnonferrous pages 2-3) |
| Hausner ratio | <1.25 for most powders tested | Fine AM powders; values concerned mainly Fe- and Ni-based powders, so this is contextual rather than Al-specific | Spierings (2018) (spierings2018powderspreadabilityand pages 115-119) |

| Static angle of repose | 26° ± 3° to 39° ± 4° | Three AlSi7Mg powders; coarser/more spherical powders gave 26–30°, while the fine, irregular powder gave 39° | Muñiz-Lerma et al. (2018) (munizlerma2018acomprehensiveapproach pages 8-11) |

| Hall flow | No flow | Fine AlSi7Mg powder, D10/D50/D90 = 14/31/58 µm | Muñiz-Lerma et al. (2018) (munizlerma2018acomprehensiveapproach pages 5-8) |
| Carney flow time | 6.1 ± 0.1 s/50 g | Coarser AlSi7Mg powders | Muñiz-Lerma et al. (2018) (munizlerma2018acomprehensiveapproach pages 5-8) |
